source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; price-level conditions rejected (shift test); this is a glossary, so most entries are pure vocabulary with no numeric test and are grouped under rejected rather than mined individually

candidates.name: Anti
candidates.quote: Anti A trade setup that attempts to enter the first pullback following a potential change of trend.
candidates.description: Enter on the first pullback that forms after price shows a potential change of trend direction.
candidates.pseudocode: trendChangeProxy(0) // e.g. close crosses the EMA against the prior trend and isFirstPullbackSinceSignal(0, maxBars)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (setup identification; actual entry is the pullback-holds test, mechanized close-then-next-open)

complexity.reason: "potential change of trend" is not defined precisely by the glossary entry; a design decision (which trend-change proxy) is needed before coding

notes: The glossary gives only the name and one-line description; the operational trend-change test and pullback depth/duration are undefined and must be chosen by the authoring pass.
Depends on the pullback primitive (G16-16).

candidates.name: ClimaxAcceleratingTrendMove
candidates.quote: Usually refers to a move near the end of an extended trend in which the trend accelerates into a steeper move, usually accompanied by an increase in volume.
candidates.description: Flags a climax: the most recent leg of the trend has moved farther, faster than the leg before it, together with an increase in volume.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(close[0] - close[legBars]) > accelMultiple * abs(close[legBars] - close[2*legBars]) and volume[0] > volumeMultiple * average(volume, volLookback)

complexity.reason: compares two successive leg magnitudes plus an average-volume gate

notes: "Exhaustion" is glossed as a synonym of climax on the same page; no separate candidate needed.

candidates.name: ComplexPullbackTwoLegAbcd
candidates.quote: A two-legged pullback that is a complete ABCD trend structure. These are common, especially in mature trends.
candidates.description: Classifies the current pullback as complex if it contains two internal counter-legs (an A-B-C-D structure) rather than one simple leg.
candidates.pseudocode: legCount(currentPullback, swingStrength) == 2

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to count internal legs within a bounded pullback window

notes: Feeds G16-25's rule-of-alternation classifier (simple vs. complex).

candidates.name: FailureTestPenetrationThenReject
candidates.quote: A type of trade in which price penetrates previous support or resistance, and then fails to continue beyond that level. This is a potentially volatile trade, but it also offers very clear risk points and profit targets.
candidates.description: Price trades through a prior support/resistance level and then closes back on the original side of it, signalling the level is holding.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < supportLevel and close[0] > supportLevel
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context test); actual entry mechanized as close-then-next-open

complexity.reason: needs an identified support/resistance level (a recent swing pivot) plus a same-bar penetrate-and-reject test

notes: "Holding" (page 448: a level the market is unable to trade beyond) and "failing" (page 447: a level failing to contain prices) are this same test's two named outcomes, not separate candidates.

candidates.name: FirstOrderPivotHighLow
candidates.quote: A pivot high is a bar that is preceded and followed by lower highs; a pivot low has higher lows before and after. These pivot points are called first-order pivots to differentiate them from more significant pivots in the market structure.
candidates.description: Definition of a confirmed swing pivot: a bar whose high (low) is higher (lower) than the N bars on either side of it.
candidates.pseudocode: high[swingStrength] > high[swingStrength - k] for all k in prior swingStrength bars, and high[swingStrength] > high[swingStrength + k] for all k in following swingStrength bars

complexity.reason: a fixed local-extreme comparison over a small, fixed window

notes: This is the plain-language definition of the swing pivot the corpus's SwingHigh/SwingLow primitives already implement, parameterized by strength; recorded here since several other glossary candidates (G16-06, G16-19, G16-21) depend on it explicitly.

candidates.name: SecondOrderPivot
candidates.quote: A pivot point that is preceded and followed by lower first-order pivots for a second-order pivot high (reversed for pivot lows).
candidates.description: A first-order swing pivot that is itself higher (for a high) than the first-order pivots immediately before and after it, i.e. a pivot of pivots.
candidates.pseudocode: firstOrderPivotHigh(pivotIndex=1) > firstOrderPivotHigh(pivotIndex=2) and firstOrderPivotHigh(pivotIndex=1) > firstOrderPivotHigh(pivotIndex=0, future)

complexity.reason: a nested pivot scan over the sequence of already-confirmed first-order pivots

notes: No exact match found in the catalog scan; existing rules take a swingStrength/pivotStrength parameter but none appear to implement a pivot-of-pivots ranking explicitly.

candidates.name: FreeBarOutsideBand
candidates.quote: Bars that are entirely outside bands or channels set on price charts—that is, with the low of the bar above the upper band or the high below the lower band.
candidates.description: The entire bar (not just the close) sits outside the Keltner band: the bar's low is above the upper band (bullish free bar).
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] > ema(close, emaLength) + bandMult * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: needs an EMA and an ATR band, tested against the whole bar rather than just the close

notes: Stricter than a close-outside-band test (mined elsewhere as CloseOutsideKeltnerBand-style rules): here the bar's LOW must clear the band, not just its close.

candidates.name: HighAndTightFlagShallowPullback
candidates.quote: A specific type of flag that holds near the high of a sharp up move (or near the low of a sharp decline) that often suggests strong buying (or selling) pressure behind the move. These often lead to sharp continuation.
candidates.description: After a sharp impulse leg, the pullback stays very shallow, holding near the impulse's extreme rather than giving back much of the move.
candidates.pseudocode: impulseRange = highest(high, impulseLookback) - lowest(low, impulseLookback); pullbackDepth(0) <= shallowFraction * impulseRange
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context test); actual entry mechanized as close-then-next-open on a pullback-holds signal

complexity.reason: needs an impulse-leg measurement plus a pullback-depth-since-extreme test

notes: No numeric shallowFraction is given by Grimes; 0.25 chosen as a reasonable 'high and tight' default.

candidates.name: ImpulseMoveLargeDirectionalBar
candidates.quote: In technical analysis, a strong movement in the market, usually sharp and in one direction. Also called a momentum move.
candidates.description: Flags a short net directional move that is large relative to recent volatility, over a small number of bars.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(close[0] - close[legBars]) > impulseAtrMult * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: a fixed-offset net-move comparison against an ATR

notes: "Momentum move" is glossed as a synonym on the same page (page 450); no separate candidate needed.

candidates.name: MicroTrendLineShortPivotWindow
candidates.quote: Micro Trendlines A term used by Al Brooks to describe very small, short-term trend lines usually drawn between two to five bars.
candidates.description: A trend line drawn between two very-close-together pivots (two to five bars apart), broken in the usual close-through-the-line way.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] < trendLine(pivotLookback, swingStrength)[0] where pivotLookback in [2,5]
candidates.book_order_type: close-based break, same as the corpus's other trend-line rules

complexity.reason: trend-line projection from pivots, same mechanism as the corpus's TrendLineBreak but with a deliberately tiny pivot window

notes: Essentially TrendLineBreak / TightChannel with pivotLookback clamped to 2-5 bars and swingStrength=1.

candidates.name: Modified3_10MacdDefinition
candidates.quote: The moving average convergence/divergence (MACD) is a standard technical indicator. This book advocates the use of a simplified, modified MACD based on 3/10/16-period moving averages.
candidates.description: Defines Grimes's modified MACD oscillator: the difference between a 3-period and a 10-period moving average, with a 16-period moving average of that difference as the signal line.
candidates.pseudocode: osc(0) = ema(close, fastLength) - ema(close, slowLength); signal(0) = ema(osc, signalLength)

complexity.reason: two moving averages plus a moving average of their difference

notes: This is the exact indicator the MINING brief's steering calls the '3/10 oscillator'; slope, zero-line-cross, and divergence tests built on this oscillator (per the steering note) are natural derived Entry candidates (osc(0) crosses above 0; osc(0) > osc(1)) but are not separately quoted here since this glossary page states only the periods, not those specific statements — the authoring pass should treat them as straightforward extensions of this primitive.
This glossary entry does not itself specify SMA vs EMA; XAverage/ema assumed by analogy with the rest of the corpus's moving-average convention.

candidates.name: MomentumDivergenceAtNewExtreme
candidates.quote: Most of them look for a new high or low in price (relative to its recent history) that is not accompanied by a new high or low on a momentum indicator, such as the MACD. The assumption is that there was less conviction behind the move, so it is more likely to fail to continue.
candidates.description: Price makes a new swing extreme, but the momentum oscillator (e.g. the 3/10 MACD) fails to make a corresponding new extreme, signalling weakening conviction.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] >= highest(high, priceLookback) and osc(0) < highest(osc, oscLookback)

complexity.reason: requires aligning a new price extreme with the oscillator's value at the prior comparable extreme, i.e. pivot-to-pivot comparison of two series

notes: No exact existing-rule name found for classic momentum divergence against a new price extreme; likely a genuinely new rule.

candidates.name: SessionOpenLocationInRange
candidates.quote: O%Rng A measure of where the open lies within the trading session's range, expressed as a percentage of that range. For instance, O%Rng of 100 percent means the open is at the high of the day's range, while 0 percent indicates the open is the low tick of that session.
candidates.description: The session's open sits in the top (or bottom) fraction of the full session's high-low range.
candidates.pseudocode: (open[0] - sessionLow(0)) / (sessionHigh(0) - sessionLow(0)) >= highThreshold

complexity.reason: needs running session high/low accessors, and compares against the FULL session range rather than the range-so-far

notes: Same construction as OpenInSessionRangeExtremeDecile (G08-27) mined in 08_trade_management.json; recorded again here since the glossary names the metric explicitly as O%Rng. Full-session range is only knowable in hindsight, so a live version must use the range-to-date as an approximation, as G08-27 does.

candidates.name: OpeningRangeDefinition
candidates.quote: A term used to describe the range price trades within a specific time following the open. Traders may use opening ranges from a few minutes to an hour.
candidates.description: Defines the opening range as the highest high and lowest low of the first N bars (or minutes) of the session, used as a breakout reference level.
candidates.pseudocode: orHigh = highest(high, orBars) over the first orBars bars of the session; orLow = lowest(low, orBars) over the same window; close[0] > orHigh
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (structural primitive); breakout mechanized as close-then-next-open

complexity.reason: a highest/lowest window anchored to the session's first N bars

notes: Grimes gives no fixed orBars; 'a few minutes to an hour' is left as a tunable parameter.

candidates.name: PriceRejectionStrongOppositeBarAtLevel
candidates.quote: Price makes an immediate (in the context of the time frame) and sharp move away from the level. The absence of price rejection suggests a higher probability of the level breaking.
candidates.description: At a support level, the bar that tests the level shows a sharp move back away from it (a long lower tail relative to the bar's range), indicating the level is holding.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] <= supportLevel and (close[0] - low[0]) > rejectionFraction * (high[0] - low[0])

complexity.reason: needs an identified support/resistance level plus a bar-shape (tail fraction) test

notes: Close cousin of G16-04 (failure test); price rejection is the bar-shape evidence for that same holding/failing outcome.

candidates.name: PullbackPrimitiveDefinition
candidates.quote: A general term for a consolidation pattern in a trend. Many of the traditional distinctions of technical analysis (flag, pennant, box, etc.) are not meaningful, as all pullback patterns can be traded according to similar rules.
candidates.description: A pullback is a counter-trend move (one or more bars against the prevailing trend direction) that has not yet produced a new trend extreme in the counter-trend direction.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] < close[1] while priorTrendDirection == up and no new trend-direction extreme has been made since the pullback began

complexity.reason: Grimes deliberately declines to give a precise numeric boundary, saying sub-distinctions (flag, pennant, box) are not meaningful; a design decision is needed to operationalize where a pullback starts and ends

notes: Foundational primitive that G16-01 (Anti), G16-03 (complex pullback), and G16-08 (high and tight flag) depend on.
"Flag" (page 447) and "retracement" (page 453) are glossed as synonyms of pullback; no separate candidates needed.

candidates.name: RangeExpansionVolatilityBreakout
candidates.quote: A market undergoing a range expansion phase will probably trend in one direction, the range of bars will probably expand, and measures of volatility will increase on some time frames.
candidates.description: Flags when the current bar's range is expanding well beyond the recent average bar range, a precursor/signal of a directional move.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] - low[0] > expansionMult * average(high - low, lookback)

complexity.reason: a single bar's range compared to a rolling average range

candidates.name: SpringSupportPenetrationRecovery
candidates.quote: The opposite of upthrusts: Price trades below support and immediately fails to carry lower. The quick recovery shows underlying buying pressure and potential accumulation.
candidates.description: Price dips below a support level and closes back above it on the same bar, a Wyckoff spring.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < supportLevel and close[0] > supportLevel
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context test); actual entry mechanized as close-then-next-open

complexity.reason: needs an identified support level (a recent confirmed swing low) plus a same-bar penetrate-and-close-back-above test

notes: The mirrored (short) side of this same rule IS Grimes's "upthrust" (page 457: "price thrusts above resistance and immediately fails to carry through... a sign of classic distribution"); recorded as one mirrored candidate rather than two separate ones, per the convention that sides mirror rather than duplicate.

candidates.name: ThreePushesReversalPattern
candidates.quote: A typical end-of-trend pattern consisting of three symmetrical (in both price and time) pushes to a new high or a new low, followed by a reversal that shows a distinct change of character.
candidates.description: Three successive swing extremes, each beyond the last, roughly matched in both price distance and bar-count spacing, followed by a reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(push3Height - push2Height) < symmetryTol * push2Height and abs(push2Height - push1Height) < symmetryTol * push1Height and abs(push3Bars - push2Bars) < timeSymmetryTol

complexity.reason: needs three ranked swing pivots plus symmetry comparisons in both price and time

candidates.name: ConfluenceMultiTimeframeLevelAlignment
candidates.quote: Some methodologies assume that support and resistance levels are more meaningful if levels from several different time frames line up at a specific price. This lining-up of levels is called confluence.
candidates.description: A support/resistance level identified on a shorter pivot window sits close to a level identified on a longer (higher-timeframe-approximating) pivot window.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(swingLow(1, strengthLTF) - swingLow(1, strengthHTF)) <= toleranceAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: needs a design decision on how many pivot ranks/windows count as separate 'timeframes' and how close is 'lined up'

notes: Per the brief's multi-timeframe convention, the higher-timeframe pivot is approximated by a stronger swingStrength/longer lookback on the same bar series rather than a literal resample.

candidates.name: TrendLegStructureImpulseRetracementImpulse
candidates.quote: In trend analysis, the third leg of the impulse-retracement-impulse unit that comprises the basic trend structure. Gauging the strength of the extension leg is one of the main ways to judge strength of the trend.
candidates.description: Defines the basic trend unit as three alternating swing legs (impulse, retracement, impulse-extension) and compares the third leg's length to the first (the 'preceding' or 'setup' leg) to judge trend strength.
candidates.pseudocode: leg3Length = abs(swingPivot(0) - swingPivot(1)); leg1Length = abs(swingPivot(2) - swingPivot(3)); leg3Length > extensionRatio * leg1Length

complexity.reason: needs three ranked, alternating swing legs and a ratio comparison between the first and third

notes: Collapses four related glossary terms into one candidate: 'extension' (p.446, the third leg), 'next trend leg' (p.451, the leg following a consolidation), 'preceding trend leg' / 'setup leg' (p.452/p.455, the leg that sets up the retracement).

candidates.name: KaufmanEfficiencyRatio
candidates.quote: The Efficiency Ratio varies from 0 to 1 and is a measure of price movement compared to noise in the market. If price moves in an unbroken line for the period, the ER would be 1. If price returns to unchanged after moving away from the starting price, the ER would be 0.
candidates.description: Kaufman's Efficiency Ratio: the net price change over a window divided by the sum of the absolute bar-to-bar changes over that same window, a directness-of-movement measure from 0 (pure noise) to 1 (unbroken line).
candidates.pseudocode: er(0) = abs(close[0] - close[erLength]) / sum(abs(close[i] - close[i-1]), i, 1, erLength)

complexity.reason: a ratio of a net move to a rolling sum of absolute bar-to-bar changes

notes: No length is given for ER in the glossary; 10 is Kaufman's own common default, adopted here.

candidates.name: ChesterKeltnerTypicalPriceChannel
candidates.quote: Originally invented by Chester Keltner, these bands were drawn around a 10-day simple moving average of the typical price, and offset by a 10-day moving average of the bars' ranges. Various modifications exist today.
candidates.description: The original Keltner band definition: an SMA of the typical price (high+low+close)/3, offset by an average of the bars' ranges (not ATR).
candidates.pseudocode: typicalPrice(0) = (high[0] + low[0] + close[0]) / 3; close[0] > average(typicalPrice, maLength) + bandMult * average(high - low, rangeLength)

complexity.reason: needs an SMA of a derived price series plus a separately averaged range band

notes: Distinct from the ATR-based Keltner (EMA of close +/- ATR multiple) mined elsewhere in the corpus and used in Grimes's own worked examples; this is Chester Keltner's original typical-price/average-range formulation. bandMult is unspecified by the glossary; defaulted to 1.0.

candidates.name: MeasuredMoveObjectiveDefinition
candidates.quote: A technique used to set an approximate price target for a swing out of consolidation, based on the assumption that future volatility will resemble past volatility. This, and all other ratio-based measures, is better used as a guide than a precise target.
candidates.description: Projects a price target for a breakout out of consolidation equal to the breakout level plus the height of the consolidation pattern that preceded it.
candidates.pseudocode: patternHeight = highest(high, patternBars) - lowest(low, patternBars); high[0] >= breakoutLevel + patternHeight
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the projected target; mechanized as a bar-extreme test

complexity.reason: needs the height of a preceding consolidation window

candidates.name: RuleOfAlternationPullbackTypeSequence
candidates.quote: In Elliott wave theory, the idea that retracements in trends tend to alternate between simple and complex consolidations.
candidates.description: The current pullback's type (simple vs. complex, per G16-03's leg count) differs from the type of the pullback immediately before it.
candidates.pseudocode: pullbackType(current) != pullbackType(previous)  // types are 'simple' (1 leg) or 'complex' (2+ legs)

complexity.reason: requires the complex-pullback leg classifier (G16-03) plus a persistent memory of the previous pullback's classification, and Elliott theory is presented as a general tendency, not a hard rule

notes: Elliott wave theory is mentioned only in passing as this glossary entry's source; Grimes does not otherwise endorse or use it elsewhere in the book, so treat this as a low-priority, speculative candidate.

candidates.name: StandardDeviationSpikeCrossRef
candidates.quote: standard deviation spike An indicator that standardizes each bar's price change for current volatility conditions.
candidates.description: Flags when the current bar's change from the prior close is an unusually large multiple of the standard deviation of daily changes over a rolling window.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(close[0] - close[1]) >= sdMultiple * stddev(close[0] - close[1], lookback)

complexity.reason: needs a standard deviation of a bar-to-bar difference series over a rolling window

notes: Same construction as G08-29 (VolatilitySpikeStdDevOfDailyChange) mined in 08_trade_management.json, where Chapter 8 gives the fuller worked description (20-day window, 3-standard-deviation color-coding threshold); recorded again here since the glossary names the indicator explicitly.

rejected.quote: adaptive markets hypothesis (AMH) A theory of market behavior pioneered by Andrew Lo that proposes that markets can be described by a process of evolving efficiency.
rejected.reason: statistics-of-the-book / academic market theory (also covers: efficient markets hypothesis and its weak/semistrong/strong forms, adaptive markets hypothesis, central limit theorem, normal distribution, bell curve, binomial tree, t-test, z-score, R-squared, linear regression, dependent/independent variable, indicator variable, null hypothesis, population, sample, significance testing, conditional/multiplicative probability, coefficient of variation, interquartile range, measures of dispersion, mean/median, variance, standard deviation, stationary, random walk hypothesis, size effect, CAPM, Modern Portfolio Theory) — no bar-level test

rejected.quote: fixed fractional risk A position-sizing plan that seeks to always risk a consistent fraction of the account's value (also called "equity" or "net liq") on each trade.
rejected.reason: position sizing (also covers: Kelly criterion, optimal f, pyramiding plans, proper pyramids, reverse pyramid, scaling in) — not a bar-level rule per the mining brief

rejected.quote: bid In financial markets, the price, often below the last price and always below the offer, where buyers are willing to purchase the asset.
rejected.reason: order-book / execution terminology (also covers: ask/offer, spread, handle, last print, limit orders, market orders, marketable limit orders, market makers, consolidated tape, high-frequency trading algorithms, good till canceled, hit the bid, pay the offer) — data the engine does not model (order book, not OHLCV)

rejected.quote: trend following ... a style of trading that usually attempts to position with a trend, with the idea that the trader may have to sit through significant whipsaws and drawdowns.
rejected.reason: describes a trading STYLE or account-activity category (also covers: always-in, black boxes, day trade, discretionary trading, systematic trading, scalping, swing trading, spread trading, pairs strategies, paper trading), not a bar-level condition

rejected.quote: candlestick chart A type of chart that pictures the space between the open and the close of a period as an empty or full rectangle...
rejected.reason: chart-format / visualization description (also covers: point and figure charts, log scale chart, linearly scaled charts, histogram chart, scatterplots), not a trading condition

rejected.quote: accumulation One of the classic market phases in which large buyers establish positions without moving the market, but also can refer to the presence of underlying buying in other contexts.
rejected.reason: Wyckoff market-phase label with no numeric test given here (also covers: distribution, markup, markdown, demand line, supply line — the trend-line-equivalent tests these last two imply are already covered by the corpus's existing trend-line rules)

rejected.quote: drawdown In trading system design or application, the amount lost from the high-water mark for the system/account. This is an underutilized measure of risk.
rejected.reason: account-equity or aggregate trade-history statistic (also covers: expectancy/expected value, excess return, risk-free rate, risk-adjusted returns, Sharpe ratio, R multiple, reward/risk ratio, economically significant, execution risk, transaction costs, slippage, disaster risks, tail risk), not a single bar-level OHLCV condition

rejected.quote: illusion of control A term that describes a person's assessment of his own skill at a task that offers random reward.
rejected.reason: trader psychology / behavioral-finance concept (also covers: futile traders, inefficient traders, theory of mind, flow, opening skew), no bar-level test

rejected.quote: trailing stop A system of trade management that moves the stop to lock in profits as the trade moves in the intended direction.
rejected.reason: cross-reference to definitions already mined with concrete numeric parameters in 08_trade_management.json (also covers: chandelier stop, stop-loss point, stop and reverse, Parabolic SAR, acceleration factor) or plain building blocks already implicit in the corpus's helpers (true range, typical price, range, moving averages) with no chapter-specific numeric refinement here

rejected.quote: Relative Strength Index (RSI) A technical indicator that seeks to identify overbought or oversold markets by measuring the relative distribution of up and down closes. Note that it does not measure relative strength, nor is it an index.
rejected.reason: names an indicator but supplies no period, threshold, or comparison to code against (also covers: ADX/DMI, relative strength, STARC bands, fast Fourier transforms, Fibonacci ratios); already covered generically by existing threshold rules (RsiBelowThreshold, RsiRising, AdxBelowThreshold, FibonacciRetracementLevel) if and when a specific threshold is chosen

rejected.quote: backtesting Applying a rule set to historical prices to see how it would have performed in terms of returns, volatility, and stability.
rejected.reason: describes research/testing methodology, not a trading condition (also covers: walk-forward testing, out-of-sample testing, Monte Carlo modeling, asynchronous trading, causation, cone of uncertainty, path-dependent)

rejected.quote: interfaces The areas between trends, trading ranges, or trends in the opposite direction. These areas can be difficult to read, but they offer some attractive trading opportunities if the risks can be properly managed.
rejected.reason: purely descriptive, non-operational market-phase concept (also covers: motive force, resistive force, market structure as a general term) with no numeric test given

chapter_summary: The glossary is the book's densest set of primitive definitions: swing pivots (first- and second-order), pullback taxonomy (simple, complex, Anti, high-and-tight flag), reversal setups at support/resistance (failure test, spring/upthrust, price rejection), trend-move vocabulary (impulse, climax/exhaustion, extension/next-leg/preceding-leg, three pushes, momentum divergence), and several precise indicator definitions (the modified 3/10/16 MACD, Chester Keltner's original typical-price channel, Kaufman's Efficiency Ratio, O%Rng, the standard-deviation-spike volatility indicator, free bars, opening range, measured move objective, confluence). Most of the roughly 150 remaining entries are pure statistics-of-the-book, position-sizing, market-microstructure/order-type, chart-format, or trading-psychology vocabulary with no bar-level test, and are grouped under a small number of rejected entries by category rather than listed individually. Two candidates here (O%Rng, standard-deviation spike) duplicate candidates already mined in 08_trade_management.json under different names; the dedup pass should merge them.
